title: Shopping and change
summary: Add up the {{term:price}}s in a basket, pay, and work out the change by counting up.
guide: When you buy more than one thing, add the {{term:price}}s first to find how much to pay altogether.

If you pay with more money than the {{term:price}}, the shopkeeper gives you change. To find it, count up from the {{term:price}} to the money you paid. From 35p to 40p is 5p, and from 40p to 50p is 10p, so the change is 15p.
100p make £1. In £3.45 the 3 is pounds and the 45 is pence: £3.45 is 345p.
Tap the money at the bottom to put it in the purse. Tap money in the purse to take it out.

pay-the-total.title: A notebook and a pen
pay-the-total.prompt: Maryam buys a notebook and a pen. Put the money for both in the purse.
pay-the-total.why: How did you decide which coins to put in?
pay-the-total.model: First I added the {{term:price}}s: 35p + 20p = 55p. Then I made 55p, for example 50p + 5p.

feedback.one-item: That pays for just one of them. Maryam is buying two things: add both {{term:price}}s.
feedback.too-big: Too much. Count the coins again.
feedback.too-small: Not enough. Add both {{term:price}}s and count again.
feedback.empty: Tap the coins at the bottom to put them in the purse.

change.title: Change
change.prompt: Ali buys a juice for 35p and pays with a 50p coin. How much change does he get? Put it in the purse.
change.hint: Count up from 35p: to 40p is how much? From 40p to 50p is how much?
change.why: How can you check your answer?
change.model: Add the {{term:price}} and the change. If you get back to the money Ali paid, it is right: 35p + 15p = 50p.

feedback.gave-price: That is the {{term:price}} of the juice. We want the money Ali gets back.
feedback.gave-paid: That is all the money Ali paid. He spent 35p of it; how much does he get back?
feedback.too-big: Too much. Add 35p to the money in the purse: it comes to more than 50p.
feedback.too-small: Not enough. Add 35p to the money in the purse: it doesn't reach 50p.
feedback.empty: Tap the coins at the bottom to put them in the purse.

count-up.title: Count up
count-up.prompt: Zahra buys bread for 65p and pays with £1. Put her change in the purse, using as few coins as you can.
count-up.why: Why does counting up from 65p to £1 give the same answer as 100 − 65?
count-up.model: Taking away finds the gap between two numbers. Counting up from 65 until I reach 100 finds that same gap: 5 and 30, which is 35. Shopkeepers often work out change like this.

feedback.gave-price: That is the {{term:price}} of the bread. We want the money Zahra gets back.
feedback.forgot-borrow: Close, but 10p too much. Count up from 65p: to 70p, then to £1.
feedback.not-fewest: 35p is right! Now make it with fewer coins.
feedback.too-big: Too much. Add 65p to the money in the purse: it comes to more than £1.
feedback.too-small: Not enough. Add 65p to the money in the purse: it doesn't reach £1.
feedback.empty: Tap the coins at the bottom to put them in the purse.

money-left.title: How much is left?
money-left.prompt: Hassan pays with £1 for a book and a pencil. How much money does he have left? Put it in the purse.
money-left.hint: First add the {{term:price}}s: 45p + 15p. Then count up to £1.
money-left.success: Well done! Hassan spent 60p and has 40p left.
money-left.why: How many steps did this problem have? Say each one.
money-left.model: Two steps. First I added the {{term:price}}s: 45p + 15p = 60p. Then I took that from £1: 100 − 60 = 40, so 40p is left.

feedback.gave-spent: 60p is the money Hassan spent. How much of his £1 is left?
feedback.one-item: Hassan bought two things. Add both {{term:price}}s first.
feedback.too-big: Too much. £1 is 100p, and 60p of it was spent.
feedback.too-small: Not enough. Add what he spent and the money in the purse: it should make £1.
feedback.empty: Tap the coins at the bottom to put them in the purse.

pounds-and-pence.title: Pounds and pence
pounds-and-pence.prompt: Sara buys a book for £3.45 and pays with a £5 note. Put her change in the purse, using as few coins as you can.
pounds-and-pence.hint: Count up from £3.45: 5p takes you to £3.50, 50p to £4, and £1 to £5.
pounds-and-pence.why: Why is it easier to count up to £5 than to work out £5.00 − £3.45 in your head?
pounds-and-pence.model: Counting up goes to easy numbers first: £3.45 → £3.50 is 5p, £3.50 → £4 is 50p, £4 → £5 is £1. Adding 5p + 50p + £1 = £1.55 needs no exchanging, but £5.00 − £3.45 means exchanging a pound for 100p.

feedback.gave-price: That is the {{term:price}} of the book. We want the money Sara gets back.
feedback.forgot-borrow: Close, but 10p too much. Count up: £3.45 → £3.50 → £4 → £5.
feedback.not-fewest: £1.55 is right! Now make it with fewer coins.
feedback.too-big: Too much. Add £3.45 to the money in the purse: it comes to more than £5.
feedback.too-small: Not enough. Add £3.45 to the money in the purse: it doesn't reach £5.
feedback.empty: Tap the coins at the bottom to put them in the purse.
